## {data-background-image="figs/NYT_Words_Disappear.jpg" data-background-size="contain" data-background-position="center" data-background-opacity="1" data-menu-title="Banned Words"}

## Institutional Racialization 

Racialization is the level to which the public and elite language used to describe an institution and its actions evoke race and thus make relevant and highlight debates around racial inequality or racial resentments.

::: {.nonincremental}
- A legacy of civil-rights era reforms? Evidence of compliance, resistance, or erosion? 
- Affected by non-white agency leaders or employees? 
- Affects responsive to racial justice claims? 
- Affects the careers of bureaucrats?
:::

::: {.notes}
But we lack a quantitative measures! 
:::
<!---alternatively, lead with theory slide--> 

## This Paper's Research Questions 

How consistent is racialization...

- in different contexts (e.g., the media, advocacy, and policymaking)? 
- over time?
- with perceived conservative or liberal ideology?

## Theory


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%" data-incremental="true"}

### Historical Institutional Racialization

<div style="border: 2px solid #2196F3; padding: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 22px;">

- Fights over racial exclusion/integration were central to the development of the federal bureaucracy  

<span style="font-style: italic; font-size: 12px; color: #333;">(King, 1999; Choi and Rainey, 2010; Schickler, 2016; Tate, 2003; White and Laird, 2020; Mansbridge, 1999; Watkins-Hayes, 2009; Minta, 2009; Juenke and Preuhs, 2012; Hayes and Hibbing, 2017)</span> 

</div>

:::

::: {.column width="33%" data-incremental="true"}


### Race & Policy Framing

<div style="border: 2px solid #2196F3; padding: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 22px;">

- Racial discourse shapes policy preferences and political behavior  

- Language brings power into focus

<span style="font-style: italic; font-size: 12px; color: #333;">(Gilens, 1999; Kellstedt, 2003; Hutchings & Valentino, 2004; Woodly, 2015; Bartels, 2020; Stephens-Dougan, L., 2020; McConnell-Ginet., 2020; Woodly, 2022; O’Brian, 2024)</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.column width="33%" data-incremental="true"}

### Race & Ideology

<div style="border: 2px solid #2196F3; padding: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 22px;">

- Perceived liberal-conservative ideology affects politics

<!--
- Agencies often become focal points of racialized policy conflict, especially in areas like civil rights and immigration  
--> 

<span style="font-style: italic; font-size: 12px; color: #333;">(Clinton and Lewis, 2008; Richardson et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2024; Epstein, 1999; Nixon, 2004; Chen and Johnson, 2014; Maranto, 2005; Maranto and Hult, 2004; Bertelli and Grose, 2011; Acs, 2025)</span>
</div>
:::

:::

# Comparing across contexts 

<!-- {data-background-image="https://ids.si.edu/ids/deliveryService?id=SAAM-2022.34_34&max=960" data-background-size="cover" data-background-opacity=".1"} -->

For each source, we have two counts: $r_{i}$ (the **count of racialized** documents/articles/sentences about agency $i$) and $y_{i}$ (the **total** document/article/sentence about agency $i$).

Share Racialized $x_i = \frac{\sqrt{r_{i}}}{\sqrt{y_{i}}}$ (variance stabilized)

Racialization Score $z_{i} = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{sd(x)}$ (standardized, mean 0, standard deviation 1)

## To Conclude {.nonincremental}

::: {.nonincremental}
- Racialization varies over time, despite stable core missions
- Perceived "centrist" agencies received less racialized attention

**Next Steps**

- Time series data for advocacy reports $\rightarrow$ Dynamic scores
- Compare with other agency ideology/partisanship measures (e.g., Chen Johnson 2015, Acs 2025, etc.)
